history.content: List every pest in Togo, then for each one list every treatment, then for each treatment list every dose, and keep going until you have nothing left.

Pest names: psyllids, aphids, caterpillars. Treatments and doses: For psyllids and aphids, spray three times around flowering: first at 30-35 days when buds appear, second ten days later, third ten days after that. For whiteflies, the same timing. For caterpillars, use a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay, dropped into the funnel; this treats about 1,500 plants with one kilogram. If insects are many, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. I will not give you an exact dose for each product.

history.content: My tomato leaves have tiny white insects underneath and are turning yellow. What is wrong and what should I do?

The whiteflies are the pest that brings yellowing of leaves and poor fruit set. Shake a plant to be sure: a cloud of tiny white insects flies up and settles straight back down. Turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before you treat at all, because a light attack does not need a spray. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them between crops. Set yellow sticky traps to catch the adults. For the approved product and its rate, see ICAT.

history.content: My cattle are weak and feverish, with pale gums and many ticks. What could it be and how do I treat them?

Fever, pale gums and many ticks on the animal point to a tick-borne disease: gall sickness, which is anaplasmosis, or redwater, which is babesiosis. Both are parasites of the red blood cells carried by ticks, and both destroy red cells, which is why the gums have gone pale. Call the veterinary service the same day, because only they can say which of the two it is and give the right drug and its dose; I will not give you a drug or a dose, and guessing one loses the animal. Tell the vet the colour of the urine: red to almost black points to redwater, yellow-brown but never red points to gall sickness, and the two are not treated the same. While you wait, keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick the ticks you can see, on the whole herd and not only on the sick animal, and never use the same needle on two animals.
